subject: Hardware fallback & graceful-degradation benchmarking — RFP follow-up
messages:
From: Alice Jordan <alice.jordan@globex.com>
To: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.ai>
Cc: procurement@globex.com
Date: 2027-08-20T09:12:00-07:00
Subject: RFP follow-up — graceful fallback behavior under contention

Hi Karthik,

Thanks for the quick turnaround on the RFP. Procurement is reviewing the risk sections and engineering needs a few specific datapoints for our benchmarking appendix. Can you provide a short, machine-readable explanation of how Redwood handles the following scenarios during heavy load or partial capacity loss? We need this for our vendor comparison table.

1) Single-GPU preemption: what happens to in-flight requests and KV cache state?
2) Model-tier fallback: if the requested model (fp16 full) is unavailable, what are the automatic/optional fallbacks and expected perf deltas?
3) Cold-start vs warmed KV cache: p50/p95/p99 token latency differences for 256-token prompts when the cache is cold vs fully warmed (no need for raw logs, just representative numbers and test method).
4) Autoscale-triggered migration: when you move traffic between nodes or regions, what is the expected tail latency spike and how do you mitigate it?

If you can return a short methodology + representative numbers and a single-page summary PDF we can append to the RFP, that would be ideal.

Best,
Alice
Alice Jordan — Senior Cloud Architect, Globex Financial
From: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.ai>
To: Alice Jordan <alice.jordan@globex.com>
Cc: Vivek Kulkarni <vivek.kulkarni@redwood.ai>, Lauren Bishop <lauren.bishop@redwood.ai>, Rishi Malhotra <rishi.malhotra@redwood.ai>, Monica Patel <monica.patel@redwood.ai>
Date: 2027-08-21T10:03:00-07:00
Subject: Re: RFP follow-up — graceful fallback behavior under contention

Alice — thanks for the clear ask. We've put together a concise methodology and representative results from our internal lab (attached: redwood-hw-fallback-exec-summary.pdf + hw-fallback-test-matrix.csv). Summary below — happy to expand any section.

Methodology (short):
- Workloads: synthetic chat generator and retrieval-augmented prompts (50/50 mix), 256 token response target.
- Sequence lengths: 32/128/256 tokens sampled to model variance; results below are for 256 tokens unless noted.
- Concurrency profile: steady-state 400 concurrent open requests with bursts to 1,600 QPS for 60s every 10 minutes.
- Test harness: closed-loop driver that simulates streaming and non-streaming clients; KV cache aging disabled except for cold-start windows.
- Hardware matrix: A100-40GB (fp16), A10G (int8 quant), CPU-only fallback (x86 64-core) for degradation cases. See hw-fallback-test-matrix.csv for exact infra combos.

Representative results (p50/p95/p99 token latency for 256-token completion; single-region, 1:1 warm caches unless noted):
- Baseline (A100, fp16, warmed cache): p50=120ms/token, p95=225ms/token, p99=390ms/token
- Fallback model (A10G, int8-quantized variant): p50=175ms/token (+46%), p95=320ms/token (+42%), p99=540ms/token (+38%)
- CPU fallback (cold path, small instance pool): p50=480ms/token, p95=930ms/token, p99=1.6s/token

Specific scenarios:
1) Single-GPU preemption: in-flight requests are immediately routed to a standby pool of compatible workers where possible. KV cache metadata (prefix hashes and chunk references) is retained in a distributed metadata service — clients may observe partial cache miss rate increase for the first ~30s while warmed state is reprovisioned; we measure a 10–20% p95 tail increase during that window in our experiments. For long-running streaming sessions we attach sticky-session TTLs to avoid hard cuts where regulatory constraints allow it.

2) Model-tier fallback: by policy you can configure automatic fallback to a quantized variant on the same hardware class or to a lower-tier model. Typical perf deltas (observed above) are 30–60% slower for int8 vs fp16 depending on prompt shape. Quality regressions are tracked via eval sets and we provide a configurable threshold that inhibits automatic fallback for top-tier traffic.

3) Cold-start vs warmed KV cache: measured p95 delta for 256-token completions: cold-start p95 ~480ms/token vs warmed p95 ~225ms/token — roughly a 2x on p95; p99 delta is larger (cold ~1.4–1.6s/token vs warmed ~390ms/token). Warm-up curves: cache hit-rate reaches >90% after approximately 1200 unique prefix requests in our sampling workload (about 8–12 minutes under steady traffic at the profile above). We include KV cache warmup traces as a short text attachment.

4) Autoscale migrations: when traffic is rebalanced between nodes or regions (e.g., draining for maintenance or to follow spot eviction) we observe transient p99 spikes of ~1.2–1.6x for 20–45s in our controlled tests. Mitigations: gradual draining, request draining TTLs, and live-model mirroring (maintain a hot replica) reduce spikes to <1.1x in the steady case. If a cross-region failover is required, expected window is 80–140s depending on network RTT and routing convergence.

Next steps: attached PDF has the one-page executive summary and the CSV includes raw runs. If Globex wants, we can run a short, customer-specific benchmark with your sample prompt set (2–4 hours) and provide CSVs and latency traces. Proposed slot: Tue 2027-08-31 13:00–16:00 PT.

Regards,
Karthik
Karthik Iyer — Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: RFP follow-up — graceful fallback behavior under contention

Alice — quick clarifications inline:

> the 80–140s cross-region window assumes DNS TTLs of 60s or a traffic-router-controlled failover?

That range covers both. 80s is our internal traffic-router-controlled failover (we maintain active egress routes and health checks and can flip within 60–90s). 140s is conservative and assumes you rely on public DNS with a 60s TTL plus BGP convergence and client-side retries. If Globex prefers, we can operate with our traffic-router for the Dedicated/Private deployment so you get the faster window and a documented SLA.

> can you provide the default policy you ship (auto-fallback enabled/disabled) and whether we can pin a traffic class to "no automatic fallback"?

Default: auto-fallback is enabled with safety thresholds. You can configure per-tenant routing policies that pin a traffic class to "no automatic fallback"; we expose that control in the Console (rollouts -> fallback policy) and via API. For compliance-sensitive traffic we recommend disabling auto-fallback and pairing with a dedicated capacity pool (we'll include the config snippet in the Drive link).

Attachments: redwood-hw-fallback-exec-summary.pdf (one-page summary), hw-fallback-test-matrix.csv (raw run matrix), kvcache-warmup-traces.txt (subset of traces). I've also pushed the CSV with p99 interruption-run details to the shared drive link and added the HubSpot note HS-94217 referencing this RFP.

If this looks good I can loop in Contracts to scope the addendum for Dedicated capacity and Traffic Router SLA.

Thanks — Karthik
